title: Alternative DAG Parameterizations
text:
Overview
Causal effect estimation from observational data often begins with uncertainty about the causal structure. A Bayesian analysis can learn about that structure and average over the remaining uncertainty, but its conclusions depend on priors whose implications for the effect of interest may be difficult to anticipate. Information about an intervention’s direction or magnitude is often easier to express than information about all the coefficients of an unknown DAG.
This book develops an effect-centered approach to Gaussian DAG models. Its organizing idea is to use a common coordinate for the same total causal effect across graphs in which that effect is possible. An ordered independence map, or I-MAP, makes the effect a coefficient in an outcome regression. Constraints on the other parameters retain the original sparse observational model. This creates a route to prior specification at the causal-effect level, while making the geometry and normalization of the remaining prior explicit.
Two inferential uses follow. A fully Bayesian workflow combines graph learning, marginal-likelihood computation, parameter sampling and model averaged effect estimation. A two-step workflow uses effect-informed structure learning to guide a separate Bayesian adjustment regression, with the adjustment set chosen according to an explicit loss. They address related questions, but need not produce the same posterior or estimator.

title: Alternative DAG Parameterizations
text:
Reading the book
The introduction explains the motivation and scientific questions (1  Introduction). Related work traces effect estimation under graph uncertainty and causal parameterization (2  Related work). Notation and context (3  Notation and context) and Bayesian preliminaries (4  Preliminaries) establish the setting. The I-MAP construction and its proofs occupy 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints. The fully Bayesian and two-step workflows are developed in 6  The fully Bayesian workflow and 7  The two-step approach. Discussion, conclusions and open questions are brought together in 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions. The appendix gives worked algebra and executable validation (Appendix A — Numerical validation and worked algebra).
Cited findings, analytical arguments, numerical checks and proposed methods have different evidential roles. A finite numerical check supports an implementation; a proof establishes a result under its assumptions. A proposed prior or algorithm requires its stated domain, normalization and inferential conditions before its properties can be assessed.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Observational compatibility and causal information
Estimating a causal effect when the causal graph is unknown brings together two sources of uncertainty: which structural relationships are present, and what their parameters imply for the intervention of interest. Structure learning and effect estimation are therefore closely connected. In Bayesian inference, the prior influences both the posterior distribution of the effect within a graph and the posterior weights assigned to different graphs.
The central aim is to develop parameterizations that permit flexible prior specification for a total causal effect when estimation also requires causal discovery. This flexibility matters for two reasons. First, prior choice can change the statistical behavior of model comparison and estimation. Non-local priors, whose densities vanish at a null effect, illustrate how the treatment of small effects can affect evidence accumulation (Johnson and Rossell 2010). Their properties in standard testing problems motivate an investigation in causal graph models; those properties do not automatically transfer to graph uncertainty or path cancellations. Second, substantive prior information is often available about an intervention’s effect rather than about the individual coefficients of an unknown DAG. A useful parameterization should make that information expressible in the quantity to which it refers.
Prior specification is particularly difficult when the graph itself is uncertain. Objective Bayesian approaches provide systematic constructions, including parameter priors designed to give the same marginal likelihood to Markov-equivalent DAGs (Geiger and Heckerman 2002; Peluso and Consonni 2020). This compatibility is valuable when the observational data do not distinguish causal orientations and the prior is intended to respect that symmetry.
There are three separate statements here. Markov-equivalent DAGs represent the same family of observational distributions, so corresponding parameter values give the same observational likelihood. Equality of their marginal likelihoods also requires compatible parameter priors. Equality of their posterior graph probabilities further requires equal prior graph probabilities. Observational equivalence alone implies neither of the latter two equalities.
Causal prior information can make a different symmetry appropriate. Consider
\[
\mathcal D_1:1\longrightarrow2\longrightarrow3,
\qquad
\mathcal D_2:1\longleftarrow2\longrightarrow3.
\]
Both graphs impose \(X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2\), yet the effect of intervening on \(X_1\) differs. In the chain, \(\tau_{13}=B_{12}B_{23}\); in the fork, \(\tau_{13}=0\) for every parameter value. Prior knowledge that this effect is nonzero is therefore information about the causal models, even though their observational families coincide. Hard prior knowledge excludes the fork; softer knowledge can be expressed through graph odds, effect distributions, or both. It does not guarantee that any finite dataset will favor the chain under every resulting prior.
A related issue is the unit on which prior symmetry is imposed. Uniform mass over DAGs generally induces unequal mass over effect hypotheses, because different hypotheses can be represented by different numbers of graphs. Even the three orientations of the same path skeleton illustrate this: only \(1\to2\to3\) permits an effect of 1 on 3, whereas \(1\leftarrow2\to3\) and \(1\leftarrow2\leftarrow3\) imply a structural zero. Equal graph masses give prior mass \(1/3\) to an active effect model and \(2/3\) to a structural null. This is a consequence of the mapping from graphs to effects, rather than a logical inconsistency. It nevertheless shows why graph-level symmetry need not express neutrality about the causal question.
An effect coordinate complements compatible-prior methods by providing another point of control. The same parameter can represent \(\tau_{dy}\) in every candidate graph with a treatment-to-outcome path. Graphs without such a path remain a separate null component. Direct control over the active-effect distribution can then be combined with an explicit prior probability of that component.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Prior choice and effect-hypothesis probabilities
A small Gaussian experiment illustrates the role of the parameter prior while keeping the graph prior fixed. Enumerate all 25 labeled DAGs on three nodes and target the effect of 1 on 3. In one scenario the true graph is \(1\to2\to3\), with both coefficients \(0.8\) and effect \(0.64\). In the other it is the collider \(1\to2\leftarrow3\), with both coefficients \(0.8\) and effect zero. Every error variance is one, and the means are known to be zero.
The baseline uses compatible DAG-Wishart shapes with \(a=8\), \(U=I_3\) and uniform graph masses. The alternative leaves the graph masses and structural-null parameter priors unchanged, and replaces each active-graph prior by the normalized non-local tilt
\[
\pi_M(\theta\mid\mathcal D)
=\frac{\tau_{13}(\theta)^2}{E_0[\tau_{13}^2\mid\mathcal D]}
\pi_0(\theta\mid\mathcal D).
\]
Thus both analyses have the same prior effect-inclusion probability \(9/25\). An active graph has a directed path from 1 to 3. Under both continuous parameter priors, exact path cancellation has probability zero, so its posterior graph mass equals \(P(\tau_{13}\ne0\mid\mathbf X)\). The tilt suppresses parameter values near a null effect within an active graph. Its normalization and graph evidences are computed exactly (Section 6.6; Section A.7). Its effect marginal remains graph dependent; this is a tractable non-local example, not a construction of a common prescribed \(h\).


Code
imap_plot_effect_testing(effect_testing_results)








Figure 1.1: Posterior probabilities of an active effect (top) and a structural null (bottom), using all 25 three-node DAGs. Lines are means over 200 replicated datasets at each size; bands are the 10th–90th percentiles across datasets, not posterior credible bands or confidence intervals for the mean. Sizes are nested within each replicate. The dotted lines show the common prior probabilities.





At \(n=1000\), the mean posterior probability of an effect under the chain is 0.344 with DAG-Wishart and 0.831 with the non-local tilt. Under the collider, the respective mean probabilities of no effect are 0.934 and 0.977. The difference arises from the parameter priors, since graph masses and likelihoods are fixed across the analyses. At the smallest size the tilt does not improve null evidence on average; the example does not establish uniform superiority.
Identification limit. The chain’s observational distribution also has a causal fork representation \(1\leftarrow2\to3\) with zero target effect: take \(B_{21}=0.8/1.64\), \(B_{23}=0.8\) and error variances \((1/1.64,1.64,1)\). These give exactly the chain covariance. Consequently the entire distribution of the plotted probabilities would be the same if that fork generated the observations. A larger posterior effect probability expresses the combination of observational evidence and prior causal assumptions; it cannot establish an orientation from observational data alone. The plot is reproducible finite simulation evidence that priors matter for hypothesis probabilities, not a proof of general testing performance or causal identification.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Two inferential workflows
The fully Bayesian workflow specifies a prior on the admissible I-MAP parameter space for each DAG, integrates its likelihood to score graphs, samples graph and parameter uncertainty, and transforms the draws into a posterior for the causal effect. Its computational requirements are substantial: an effect coefficient must be accompanied by a proper nuisance prior, a tractable marginal likelihood and a parameter sampler. The I-MAP construction provides the coordinate and model constraints; establishing unrestricted effect-prior specification and efficient computation is a further inferential problem.
The two-step workflow separates structure learning from effect estimation. Effect-informed graph learning supplies a distribution over candidate causal structures. A subsequent Bayesian regression uses an adjustment set chosen for the inferential objective. The intended link is a common prior on the active causal effect in both steps. This leaves room to choose adjustment sets by a prespecified loss, rather than fixing the regression to the original DAG parent set. Matching one prior marginal does not make the two procedures identical: their nuisance models and use of the data must also be specified.
The setting throughout is a fully observed, acyclic linear Gaussian system with independent errors, one treatment and one outcome. The original DAG is assumed to be causal. Gaussian factorization enables the construction, but does not remove observational ambiguity about that causal graph.

title: 2  Related work
text:
2.1 From IDA to effect inference under graph uncertainty
Pearl’s graphical framework connects conditional independence, structural equations and interventions (Pearl 1988, 2009). With observational data and the usual causal sufficiency and faithfulness assumptions, a discovery procedure can identify a Markov equivalence class rather than a unique causal DAG. The IDA algorithm of Maathuis, Kalisch and Bühlmann addresses the resulting effect ambiguity: it combines an estimated equivalence class with local parent-set possibilities to estimate a collection of possible intervention effects in linear systems (Maathuis et al. 2009). These possibilities are not posterior probabilities, and repeated estimates need not represent distinct causal functionals.
Several branches develop this starting point. Joint-IDA extends effect estimation to simultaneous interventions, where intervening on one treatment changes paths from another (Nandy et al. 2017). Ancestral-graph methods extend possible-effect reasoning to settings that allow latent variables, under different graphical assumptions (Malinsky and Spirtes 2016). Neither extension can be obtained by applying a single-treatment, causally sufficient formula unchanged.
The adjustment branch asks when an observational regression identifies a causal effect across compatible graphs. Perković, Textor, Kalisch and Maathuis give a complete graphical characterization of adjustment sets for DAGs and several partially directed or ancestral graph classes (Perković et al. 2018). Incorporating background knowledge leads to maximally oriented partially directed acyclic graphs (MPDAGs), for which Perković develops a broader identification criterion (Perković 2020). Identification by the g-formula can be possible even when adjustment alone is insufficient. Guo and Perković further partition a graph class by distinct identified effect functionals, reducing duplication in enumeration (Guo and Perković 2021).
A second branch concerns efficiency after identification. Henckel, Perković and Maathuis establish graphical variance comparisons and the O-set’s asymptotic optimality among valid least-squares adjustment estimators in causal linear models (Henckel et al. 2022). Witte, Henckel, Maathuis and Didelez interpret this set through forbidden projection and use it for efficient estimation of possible effects (Witte et al. 2020). These findings motivate the outcome-parent set in the I-MAP construction. Their optimality is within an adjustment-estimator class: Guo and Perković show that recursive least squares can exploit additional linear-model restrictions and is efficient among regular estimators based on the sample covariance (Guo and Perković 2022). Guo, Perković and Rotnitzky study elimination of variables while retaining identification and the semiparametric efficiency bound for an interventional mean (Guo et al. 2023).
Further developments address conditional effects and the causal consequences of discovery errors. LaPlante and Perković characterize conditional adjustment in MPDAGs and PAGs when conditioning variables are unaffected by treatment (LaPlante and Perković 2024). Their preprint on conditional identification goes beyond adjustment to a complete identification algorithm in MPDAGs (LaPlante and Perković 2025). A separate preprint by LaPlante, Triantafillou and Perković provides data-driven routes to adjustment for multiple treatments under restrictions on the adjustment variables (LaPlante et al. 2025). These results concern identification criteria, not automatic correction for all uncertainty introduced by estimating a graph from finite data.
Henckel, Würtzen and Weichwald propose adjustment identification distances that assess learned structures through the causal formulas they imply (Henckel et al. 2024). Wienöbst, Henckel and Weichwald develop discrete score-based search with iterative Cholesky updates (Wienöbst et al. 2026). Freni, Henckel and Weichwald’s verification preprint asks whether a given observational formula identifies an intervention distribution, a question distinct from finding some identifying formula (Freni et al. 2026). Together, these strands connect identification, efficient estimation and computational discovery. They do not supply a common prior on an effect across unknown DAGs, which is the inferential role considered here.

section: 2.2 Bayesian structure learning and causal effect estimation
text:
2.2 Bayesian structure learning and causal effect estimation
Bayesian methods give weights to graph and parameter uncertainty rather than only enumerating possible effects. Castelletti and Consonni develop Gaussian causal effect inference with unknown structure (Castelletti and Consonni 2021). Castelletti and Mascaro consider joint interventions among network-dependent variables (Castelletti and Mascaro 2021). Pensar and colleagues provide another Bayesian route to observational effect inference (Pensar et al. 2020), and Castelletti, Consonni and Della Vedova develop a categorical-model workflow (Castelletti et al. 2024).
For Gaussian models, DAG-Wishart priors provide conjugate integration and parameter sampling (Ben-David et al. 2015). Peluso and Consonni construct compatible priors for comparing DAG models (Peluso and Consonni 2020), building on the parameter-prior framework of Geiger and Heckerman (Geiger and Heckerman 2002). The resulting evidence and averaging calculations are explained in Chapter 4. Their practicality is a useful benchmark for an effect-centered alternative.
Non-local priors make prior density vanish at a null parameter value and can alter Bayes-factor learning rates under stated testing assumptions (Johnson and Rossell 2010). This motivates separating structural null effects from active effects and controlling the latter near zero. The exact reweighting identity in Section 6.6 is available for a normalized effect tilt; claims about graph-selection consistency or effect-estimation performance require additional analysis.

title: 2  Related work
text:
2.3 Frugal parameterization
Evans and Didelez organize a joint model around a causal distribution, together with a distribution for the remaining variables and a conditional association component (Evans and Didelez 2024). Under their assumptions, this yields a smooth, regular and non-redundant parameterization. Appropriate association measures, such as odds ratios or copulas, can supply variation independence. Their framework supports simulation and likelihood-based inference, including Bayesian inference, and extends beyond Gaussian mean effects to marginal causal distributions and longitudinal models.
Three properties need to be distinguished. Non-redundancy means that distinct admissible parameter values do not encode the same distribution. Variation independence means that parameter blocks can vary over a Cartesian product of their separate ranges. Saturation means that a model contains every distribution in the specified observational family. A parameterization can be non-redundant without being saturated or variation independent. In the paper’s Gaussian example, a regression coefficient for the association component entails a variance inequality; using an appropriate correlation removes that dependence in the saturated model (Evans and Didelez 2024, Example 1.2).
Steiner and Steel connect variation independence with the convenience of assigning independent priors to the frugal blocks (Steiner and Steel 2024). Their Bayesian example concerns a model with independently specifiable blocks. A sparse observational DAG can impose additional relations across those blocks. The question for structure learning is therefore whether the desired independent prior remains supported on each candidate sparse model, not whether the unrestricted frugal construction permits Bayesian inference.

2.3.1 A sparse chain: constraints without redundancy
Analytical example. Consider the centered Gaussian chain
\[
X_1=\epsilon_1,\qquad X_2=bX_1+\epsilon_2,\qquad
X_3=cX_2+\epsilon_3,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_j)=v_j>0,
\]
with mutually independent errors. The target is the effect of 1 on 3, \(\tau_{13}=bc\). Write \(s=c^2v_2+v_3\). Since treatment 1 has no parents,
\[
X_3\mid\operatorname{do}(X_1=x)\sim N(\tau_{13}x,s)
\]
also equals its observational conditional distribution given \(X_1=x\).
A Gaussian marginal-and-association representation of all three variables is
\[
X_1\sim N(0,v_1),\qquad X_2\mid X_1\sim N(bX_1,v_2),
\]
\[
X_3\mid X_1,X_2\sim
N\{\tau X_1+\alpha(X_2-bX_1),\ s-\alpha^2v_2\}.
\]
Marginalizing over \(X_2\mid X_1\) gives \(X_3\mid X_1\sim N(\tau X_1,s)\). Thus \((v_1,b,v_2)\) describes \(p(x_1,x_2)\), \((\tau,s)\) describes the marginal effect model, and \(\alpha\) describes residual association. Here \(X_2\) is a mediator, not a pretreatment covariate: the integration weight is \(p(x_2\mid x_1)\), rather than a baseline marginal \(p(x_2)\). This is a marginal-and-association special case of the frugal construction; the usual pretreatment adjustment recipe cannot be used unchanged.
On the saturated Gaussian family, the domain is \(v_1,v_2,s>0\) and \(s>\alpha^2v_2\), with \(b,\tau\in\mathbb R\). Expanding the conditional mean shows that the direct coefficient of \(X_1\) in the outcome equation is \(\tau-\alpha b\). The chain’s missing edge \(1\to3\) therefore imposes exactly
\[
\tau=\alpha b.
\]
On this constrained domain, the original coefficients and variances are recovered uniquely:
\[
c=\alpha,\qquad v_3=s-\alpha^2v_2.
\]
The chain has five free parameters, and the six ambient coordinates satisfy one independent equation. There is no duplication of distributions. Ignoring the equation would fit the saturated model instead of the chain.
To separate this constraint from the variance inequality, use
\[
\rho=\alpha\sqrt{v_2/s},\qquad -1<\rho<1.
\]
This is the correlation of \(X_2-bX_1\) with \(X_3-\tau X_1\). In the ambient model, \((v_1,b,v_2)\), \((\tau,s)\) and \(\rho\) have a Cartesian-product domain. On the chain, however,
\[
\tau=b\rho\sqrt{s/v_2},\qquad
c=\rho\sqrt{s/v_2},\qquad v_3=s(1-\rho^2).
\]
The restricted parameterization remains injective, but the effect cannot vary independently of these particular nuisance coordinates. If \(b=0\), the effect is necessarily zero. Where \(b\ne0\), \((\tau,b,v_1,v_2,v_3)\) gives an alternative chart, with \(c=\tau/b\) and absolute inverse Jacobian \(1/|b|\). That chart excludes valid points with \(b=0\); at \(b=c=0\), the differential of \(bc\) vanishes, so \(\tau\) cannot be a coordinate in a smooth local chart of the full five-dimensional model.
For the distinct target effect of 2 on 3, node 1 is a pretreatment variable. Applying the elementary frugal recipe with \(Z=X_1\), treatment \(X_2\) and outcome \(X_3\) sets the residual \(Z\)-outcome association to zero and retains the five free parameters. This gives another sparse, non-redundant example.
Consequently, a complete DAG is not necessary for non-redundancy. Missing edges restrict the admissible frugal coordinates, and may destroy their blockwise variation independence. The practical comparison with I-MAP coordinates concerns how these restrictions are constructed and handled across a graph search, rather than an inherent redundancy of frugal parameterization.


2.3.2 The shared prior-specification difficulty
Proposition (loss of variation independence in the displayed blocks). In the chain, the Gaussian frugal blocks \(\theta_{12}=(v_1,b,v_2)\), \(\theta_{3\mid\operatorname{do}(1)}=(\tau,s)\) and \(\rho\) are not jointly variation independent. The equivalent I-MAP entries are also constrained. Independent, non-degenerate continuous priors on all of either representation’s ambient entries assign probability zero to the chain model.






NoteProof





The frugal relation is \(\tau=b\rho\sqrt{s/v_2}\). At fixed \(b,v_2,s\), it requires
\[
|\tau|<|b|\sqrt{s/v_2}\quad(b\ne0),\qquad \tau=0\quad(b=0).
\]
For example, \(b=v_2=s=1\) cannot be combined with \(\tau=2\), although each block value separately occurs in an admissible chain. Thus the joint domain is not the product of its block projections. The missing-edge equation determines one coordinate and has probability zero under independent ambient densities.
For the I-MAP ordering \((1,3,2)\), write
\[
X_3=tX_1+e_3^*,\qquad X_2=rX_1+kX_3+e_2^*,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e_3^*)=s,\quad\operatorname{Var}(e_2^*)=u>0.
\]
Restoring the chain gives \(b=r+kt\), \(v_2=u+k^2s\), \(c=ks/(u+k^2s)\) and \(v_3=su/(u+k^2s)\). Its missing direct edge requires \(t=bc\), equivalently
\[
tu=rks.
\]
This likewise determines \(t\) at fixed \(r,k,s,u\), and is a probability-zero equation under independent ambient densities. Both restrictions encode the same original chain. \(\square\)



Solving the frugal constraint for \(\rho\) leaves the domain \(s>\tau^2v_2/b^2\) when \(b\ne0\). An arbitrary effect density \(h(\tau)\) and independent nuisance density \(g(b,v_1,v_2,s)\) will generally put mass outside this domain. Simply restricting their product and normalizing it globally changes the effect marginal to
\[
\frac{h(t)A(t)}{\int h(z)A(z)\,dz},\qquad
A(t)=\int\mathbf1\{s>t^2v_2/b^2\}\,g(b,v_1,v_2,s)\,d(b,v_1,v_2,s).
\]
Whenever \(A(t)>0\), a nuisance density normalized conditional on \(t\) can preserve \(h\). The same need for an admissible domain, conditional normalization and chart Jacobian occurs in constrained I-MAP coordinates (Chapter 6).
This is a shared constraint-handling problem, not a universal impossibility of prescribing an effect prior. On \(b\ne0\), the chart \((\tau,b,v_1,v_2,v_3)\) has a product domain and \(c=\tau/b\); it supports independent proper priors on those coordinates. The omitted \(b=0\) boundary has zero probability under a continuous prior on \(b\), although division by small \(b\) can matter computationally. No smooth chart containing the effect as a coordinate covers \(b=c=0\), where its differential vanishes. Nor does every missing edge destroy variation independence: the target 2-on-3 example above has an independent effect coefficient. A complete DAG is therefore not a necessary condition for variation independence either; the result depends on the target, the blocks and the sparse constraints.

title: 3  Notation and context
text:
3.1 Graphs and Gaussian models
The graph describes the causal system, while a variable ordering describes an observational regression factorization. Keeping these objects distinct is essential: changing the ordering can expose a causal effect without giving every new arrow a causal interpretation.
The symbol \(\pi\) without a subscript denotes an ordering; \(\pi_{\mathcal D}(\theta)\) denotes a density. Parent sets are \(P_j=\operatorname{pa}_{\mathcal D}(j)\), whereas all predecessors in an ordering are \(R_j^\pi\). Matrices retain the original node labels unless a permutation is stated explicitly.
Let \(\mathcal D=(V,E)\) be a DAG on \(V=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Write \(\operatorname{pa}_{\mathcal D}(j)\), \(\operatorname{an}_{\mathcal D}(j)\) and \(\operatorname{de}_{\mathcal D}(j)\) for parents, strict ancestors and strict descendants. These sets exclude the node itself. An ordering is topological when every parent precedes its children. For a set, parents and ancestors denote unions of the corresponding node sets.
Use \(\mathcal D\) for the graph and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(v_1,\ldots,v_q)\) for positive error variances. The centered structural equations are
\[
X=B^\top X+\epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim N_q(0,D),\qquad L=I-B,
\]
where \(B_{uj}=0\) if \(u\notin\operatorname{pa}_{\mathcal D}(j)\). Allowed edge coefficients may equal zero; requiring every allowed coefficient to be nonzero would unnecessarily exclude legitimate parameter values and would still not guarantee faithfulness. Consequently,
\[
L^\top X=\epsilon,\qquad
\Sigma=L^{-\top}DL^{-1},\qquad \Omega=LD^{-1}L^\top.
\]
All errors are mutually independent. There are no hidden variables, selection effects, or feedback loops. Means are assumed known to be zero in the likelihood calculations. Estimating an intercept or mean requires changing those calculations and their parameter counts.

title: 3  Notation and context
text:
3.2 Interventions and total effects
A hard intervention \(\operatorname{do}(X_d=x)\) replaces the equation for \(X_d\) by the constant \(x\) and removes its incoming edges. The remaining structural equations are retained. For \(d\ne y\), define
\[
\tau_{dy}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}E[X_y\mid\operatorname{do}(X_d=x)]
=\sum_{p:d\rightsquigarrow y}\prod_{(u\to v)\in p} B_{uv}
=[L^{-1}]_{dy}.
\]






NoteProof





Since \(B\) is nilpotent after topological permutation, \((I-B)^{-1}=I+B+\cdots+B^{q-1}\). For distinct endpoints its \((d,y)\) entry enumerates the directed paths. Replacing the treatment equation yields the same propagation along paths starting at \(d\).



If no directed path exists, \(\tau_{dy}=0\) for all parameters. If a path exists, opposing path contributions may still cancel. Thus ancestry and a nonzero effect are different statements at particular parameter values. For simultaneous interventions, paths through another intervened treatment are removed; the single-treatment formula cannot be reused without this change. Joint interventions require a separate construction (Nandy et al. 2017; Castelletti and Mascaro 2021).

title: 3  Notation and context
text:
3.3 Adjustment and the O-set
A set \(Z\subseteq V\setminus\{d,y\}\) is valid for adjustment if, for every causal distribution compatible with the original DAG,
\[
p(x_y\mid\operatorname{do}(X_d=x))
=\int p(x_y\mid X_d=x,X_Z=z)p(z)\,dz.
\]
For \(Z=\varnothing\), the right side is \(p(x_y\mid X_d=x)\). In a Gaussian model write the observational conditional mean as
\[
E[X_y\mid X_d,X_Z]=\beta_d X_d+\beta_Z^\top X_Z.
\]
If \(Z\) is valid, integrating this expression proves \(\beta_d=\tau_{dy}\). The adjustment identity does not generally equate the observational conditional law with \(p(x_y\mid\operatorname{do}(X_d=x),X_Z=z)\) for an arbitrary valid set.
Suppose \(d\in\operatorname{an}_{\mathcal D}(y)\) and let
\[
M=\operatorname{de}_{\mathcal D}(d)\cap\operatorname{an}_{\mathcal D}(y),\qquad
C=M\cup\{y\},\qquad
O=\operatorname{pa}_{\mathcal D}(C)\setminus(\{d\}\cup M).
\]
The general O-set definition removes the treatment and the causal nodes together with their descendants. In this single-treatment DAG setting, an external parent of \(C\) cannot be a descendant of \(C\) without a directed cycle, so it reduces to the displayed expression. An external parent descended from \(d\) would itself lie in \(M\); hence \(O\) contains only non-descendants of \(d\).
Source-supported result. The O-set is valid and minimizes the asymptotic variance of the OLS total-effect estimator over valid adjustment sets under the causal linear-model assumptions (Henckel et al. 2022; Witte et al. 2020). This is not a claim of universal finite-sample or Bayesian optimality. With \(A=(d,O)\) in that order,
\[
\tau_{dy}=[\Sigma_{AA}^{-1}\Sigma_{Ay}]_1,\qquad
\widehat\tau_{dy}=[S_{AA}^{-1}S_{Ay}]_1.
\]
\(S\) is the sample covariance matrix (centered when fitting an intercept). Equivalently, use \((W^\top W)^{-1}W^\top x_y\) for the regression design \(W\). The asymptotic variance is
\[
\operatorname{avar}(\widehat\tau_{dy})=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_y\mid X_d,X_O)}{n\operatorname{Var}(X_d\mid X_O)}.
\]

title: 3  Notation and context
text:
3.4 Independence maps and ordered regressions
Let \(\mathcal I(\mathcal D)\) denote all graphical d-separations, and \(\mathcal I(p)\) all distributional conditional independences. A DAG \(G\) is an I-MAP of \(p\) if \(\mathcal I(G)\subseteq\mathcal I(p)\), and an I-MAP of \(\mathcal D\) if \(\mathcal I(G)\subseteq\mathcal I(\mathcal D)\). This latter definition does not require choosing a faithful distribution. Faithfulness means \(\mathcal I(p)=\mathcal I(\mathcal D)\).
For ordering \(\pi\), put \(R_{\pi_j}^\pi=\{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{j-1}\}\), the predecessors of the node \(\pi_j\). Define the ordered graph by
\[
\pi_i\to\pi_j\in G^\pi_{\mathcal D}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
i<j\ \text{and}\ \pi_i\not\!\perp_{\mathcal D}\pi_j\mid R_{\pi_j}^\pi\setminus\{\pi_i\}.
\]
The edge criterion uses dependence. For nonsingular Gaussians, the corresponding distribution-specific construction keeps exactly the nonzero coefficients in each regression on all predecessors. Gaussian conditional independence satisfies the intersection property, so removing all zero coefficients leaves a valid factorization. Each retained coefficient is necessary: deleting it would impose a conditional independence that fails in that regression. Thus the distribution-specific graph is a minimal I-MAP. Taking a faithful Gaussian distribution of \(\mathcal D\) gives the graphical ordered minimal I-MAP above; its definition applies to the entire DAG model.
Minimal means no edge can be removed while retaining the I-MAP property; it does not mean globally fewest edges. At unfaithful parameter values, a regression coefficient can vanish on an edge of the graph-defined I-MAP. Keep the graph and its allowed coefficients separate.

title: 4  Preliminaries
text:
4.1 Bayesian causal inference with an unknown DAG
A conventional Bayesian analysis places a mass function \(p(\mathcal D)\) on a specified DAG space \(\mathfrak D\) and a parameter prior \(\pi_{0,\mathcal D}(\theta)\) on each graph’s Gaussian model. The observational likelihood is
\[
p(\mathbf X\mid\theta,\mathcal D)
=(2\pi)^{-nq/2}\prod_{j=1}^q v_j^{-n/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac12\sum_{j=1}^q\frac{1}{v_j}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(x_{ij}+\sum_{u\in P_j}L_{uj}x_{iu}\right)^2\right\}.
\]
Here means are known to be zero, as in Chapter 3. The marginal likelihood integrates over the free coefficients and positive variances:
\[
m_0(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)=\int_{\Theta_{\mathcal D}}
p(\mathbf X\mid\theta,\mathcal D)\pi_{0,\mathcal D}(\theta)\,d\theta.
\]
Bayes’ rule yields
\[
p_0(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf X)=
\frac{m_0(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)p(\mathcal D)}
{\sum_{\mathcal D'\in\mathfrak D}m_0(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D')p(\mathcal D')}.
\]
For a small graph space the sum can be evaluated directly. Larger spaces usually require a search or a graph sampler, using scores and proposal probabilities rather than enumerating every DAG. Conditional on a sampled DAG, draw its parameters from the corresponding posterior and compute \(\tau_{dy}(\mathcal D,\theta)\). This is the basic graph-and-parameter averaging architecture of Bayesian effect inference (Castelletti and Consonni 2021; Castelletti and Mascaro 2021; Pensar et al. 2020).

title: 4  Preliminaries
section: 4.2 From parameter posteriors to an effect posterior
text:
4.2 From parameter posteriors to an effect posterior
For any measurable effect set \(A\),
\[
P_0(\tau_{dy}\in A\mid\mathbf X)=
\sum_{\mathcal D\in\mathfrak D}p_0(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf X)
\int_{\Theta_{\mathcal D}}\mathbf1\{\tau_{dy}(\mathcal D,\theta)\in A\}
\pi_{0,\mathcal D}(\theta\mid\mathbf X)\,d\theta.
\]
The same operation induces the prior effect distribution before observing data. In ordinary edge coordinates, the active effect is a path-sum polynomial. Its induced distribution depends on the graph, its number and arrangement of paths, and its coefficient prior. Even identical local coefficient priors can therefore give different effect distributions in different DAGs.
Graphs without a directed \(d\)-to-\(y\) path contribute a point mass at zero. Under continuous coefficient priors, path cancellation in an ancestor graph has probability zero, although the parameter space includes such values. Thus a typical averaged effect posterior combines a structural-null atom with continuous active-effect components. Graph uncertainty persists within a Markov equivalence class unless prior or additional causal information distinguishes its members.

title: 4  Preliminaries
text:
4.3 Exact DAG-Wishart baseline
The DAG-Wishart distribution is a conjugate prior for Gaussian DAG models (Ben-David et al. 2015; Peluso and Consonni 2020). In the \(L=I-B\) convention, its normalization follows by completing the square. For centered independent observations collected in an \(n\times q\) matrix \(\mathbf X\), take \(U\succ0\) and shape vector \(\alpha\) with \(\alpha_j>|P_j|+2\), \(P_j=\operatorname{pa}_{\mathcal D}(j)\). The prior density with respect to the free entries of \(L\) and the variances is
\[
\pi(L,D\mid\mathcal D)=\frac1{Z_{\mathcal D}(\alpha,U)}
\exp\{-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(LD^{-1}L^\top U)\}
\prod_j v_j^{-\alpha_j/2}.
\]
Put \(p_j=|P_j|\), \(K_j=U_{P_jP_j}\), \(u_j=U_{P_jj}\), \(s_j=U_{jj}-u_j^\top K_j^{-1}u_j\), and \(r_j=(\alpha_j-p_j)/2-1\). Empty parent sets have determinant one and \(s_j=U_{jj}\). Completing the square in the exponent and then integrating the variance gives
\[
Z_{\mathcal D}(\alpha,U)=\prod_j
(2\pi)^{p_j/2}|K_j|^{-1/2}\Gamma(r_j)(s_j/2)^{-r_j}.
\]






NoteProof





Indeed the coefficient integral contributes \((2\pi v_j)^{p_j/2}|K_j|^{-1/2}\), and the remaining integral is that of an inverse-gamma kernel.



Equivalently, independently over nodes,
\[
v_j\sim\operatorname{IG}(r_j,s_j/2),\qquad
L_{P_jj}\mid v_j\sim N(-K_j^{-1}u_j,v_jK_j^{-1}).
\]
Here \(\operatorname{IG}(r,b)\) has density \(b^r\Gamma(r)^{-1}v^{-r-1}e^{-b/v}\). Marginally the coefficient vector is Student \(t\) with \(2r_j\) degrees of freedom, center \(-K_j^{-1}u_j\), and scale matrix \(s_jK_j^{-1}/(2r_j)\); that scale is not its covariance matrix.
The posterior updates are \(\alpha_j\mapsto\alpha_j+n\) and \(U\mapsto U+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\). Thus
\[
m_0(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)=(2\pi)^{-nq/2}
\frac{Z_{\mathcal D}(\alpha+n\mathbf1,U+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)}{Z_{\mathcal D}(\alpha,U)}.
\]
A compatible choice is \(\alpha_j=a-q+2p_j+3\) with \(a>q-1\) and common \(U\), yielding the score-equivalent construction discussed by Peluso and Consonni. The scalar \(a\) is a shape hyperparameter; \(U\) is the scale/rate matrix in the exponential kernel. Arbitrary DAG-Wishart shapes need not yield equal marginal likelihoods for Markov-equivalent graphs.

title: 4  Preliminaries
text:
4.4 Compatibility and what it controls
With compatible parameter priors, equivalent observational models have equal integrated scores. This provides a controlled baseline for graph comparison. It does not prescribe equal prior mass for active and null causal-effect hypotheses, and it does not directly specify the active-effect marginal. A prior informed by causal knowledge can intentionally depart from score equivalence, provided its meaning and normalization are clear.
The I-MAP workflow retains the same likelihood and averaging architecture. Its departure lies in how the prior is organized around the causal effect, and in the integration and sampling needed for that prior. The exact conjugate score above supplies a benchmark for those computations; reparameterizing a fixed prior must reproduce it.

title: 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints
text:
5.1 Existence of a closest ordering
Assume the setting of Chapter 3 with \(d\in\operatorname{an}_{\mathcal D}(y)\). A closest ordering has the form
\[
\pi_{dy}=\langle\delta_1,d,M,y,\delta_3\rangle,
\]
where the mediator block \(M\) is internally topological. Such an ordering always exists.
Move \(y\) just before the mediator block to obtain
\[
\pi^*=\langle\delta_1,d,y,M,\delta_3\rangle.
\]
Different choices inside \(\delta_1,M,\delta_3\) may give different I-MAPs. “Optimal” here refers to the outcome regression’s adjustment efficiency; it does not identify a unique globally optimal graph.

title: 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints
text:
NoteProof





Define \(S=\{d\}\cup M\cup\{y\}\) and \(A=\operatorname{an}_{\mathcal D}(S)\setminus S\). Choose a topological ordering within \(A\), then \(d,M,y\), then the remaining nodes. This is topological: every outside parent of \(S\) belongs to \(A\), and an ancestor of \(S\) descended from \(d\) must lie on a \(d\)-to-\(y\) path and so belongs to \(S\). No node in \(S\) can therefore be an ancestor of a node in \(A\). Since \(A\cup S\) is ancestral, all remaining nodes can be placed last. This establishes the existence of a closest ordering.

title: 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints
section: 5.2 Outcome parents and the effect coordinate
text:
5.2 Outcome parents and the effect coordinate
Proposition (outcome parents and effect coordinate). For any closest ordering, the graph-defined ordered minimal I-MAP \(G^*=G^{\pi^*}_{\mathcal D}\) has
\[
\operatorname{pa}_{G^*}(y)=\{d\}\cup O.
\]
For every positive-variance parameter value of the original Gaussian DAG model, including unfaithful ones, its regression factorization in \(\pi^*\) satisfies
\[
-\widetilde L_{dy}=\tau_{dy}.
\]






NoteProof





Every external parent of \(M\cup\{y\}\) is either \(d\) or lies in \(O\subseteq\delta_1\). Successive substitution of the equations for the mediators therefore gives
\[
X_y=\tau_{dy}X_d+\sum_{u\in O}c_uX_u+\eta,
\]
where \(\eta\) is a linear combination of the errors at \(M\cup\{y\}\). Because the closest ordering is topological, \((X_{\delta_1},X_d)\) depends only on earlier errors, so \(\eta\) is independent of this entire predecessor vector. Its variance is positive because its coefficient on \(\epsilon_y\) is one. This is exactly the regression of \(X_y\) on \((X_{\delta_1},X_d)\); all predecessors outside \(\{d\}\cup O\) have zero coefficients.
For each \(u\in O\), an edge \(u\to c\), \(c\in M\cup\{y\}\), followed by a directed path from \(c\) to \(y\) supplies a monomial in \(c_u\). All internal nodes of this path lie in the mediator block. Distinct paths give distinct monomials with positive formal signs in the \(B\) coefficients; hence \(c_u\) is not the zero polynomial. Likewise, a directed \(d\)-to-\(y\) path makes \(\tau_{dy}\) a nonzero polynomial. These coefficients can be nonzero in the DAG model and thus their associated conditional independences are not graphically implied. By the ordered edge criterion, precisely these predecessor nodes are parents in \(G^*\). This proves the graph statement, while the substitution identity proves the effect equality at all parameter values. \(\square\)



Ancestors of \(d\) need not be separated from the outcome by conditioning on \(d\). For example, \(u\to d\), \(u\to y\) and \(d\to y\) leave \(u\) associated with \(y\) given \(d\). Such confounders are included in the external-parent regression.

title: 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints
text:
5.3 Adjacent transposition
Let \(i,j\) be adjacent in the current factorization ordering, with \(i\) preceding \(j\), and put \(a=L_{ij}\). It is permissible that \(a=0\). Save the old variances \(v_i,v_j\) and set \(s=v_j+a^2v_i\). Apply these column operations in sequence:
\[
L_{\cdot j}^{E}=L_{\cdot j}-aL_{\cdot i},\qquad
\widetilde L_{\cdot i}=L_{\cdot i}+\frac{av_i}{s}L_{\cdot j}^{E},\qquad
\widetilde L_{\cdot j}=L_{\cdot j}^{E},
\]
and leave other columns unchanged. The new variances are
\[
\widetilde v_i=\frac{v_iv_j}{s},\qquad \widetilde v_j=s.
\]
Swap \(i,j\) in the ordering. Both variance updates use the old values; an in-place update that reuses the new \(v_i\) in \(s\) is incorrect.






NoteProof of covariance preservation and DAG validity





The eliminated error is \(\epsilon_j^E=\epsilon_j-a\epsilon_i\), with variance \(s\) and covariance \(-av_i\) with \(\epsilon_i\). Replacing the latter by \(\widetilde\epsilon_i=\epsilon_i+(av_i/s)\epsilon_j^E\) makes these two errors uncorrelated, hence independent by Gaussianity, and gives variance \(v_iv_j/s\). The invertible equation operations leave \(X\) unchanged, so
\[
\widetilde L^{-\top}\widetilde D\widetilde L^{-1}=L^{-\top}DL^{-1}.
\]
Adjacency ensures that both old columns involve only predecessors and the pair itself. After elimination the \(j\) column involves only earlier nodes; the \(i\) column involves those nodes and \(j\). The unit diagonal is retained and the new matrix is triangular in the swapped ordering. Its equations therefore constitute a DAG factorization. Uniqueness of Gaussian regressions on all predecessors identifies it with the modified Cholesky factorization in that ordering. \(\square\)



The covariance algebra alone is insufficient to establish a DAG for arbitrary \(i\to j\). In \(i\to k\to j\) with \(i\to j\), transposing \(i,j\) can introduce \(k\to i\) while retaining \(i\to k\). Adjacency is essential to DAG validity. Minimality follows from the ordered construction: for a faithful input distribution, numerical nonzero support gives the ordered minimal I-MAP; for a graph-defined output use d-separation in the original graph, rather than thresholding a particular parameter matrix.

title: 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints
text:
5.4 Forward and reverse algorithms
The forward construction is summarized in Algorithm 5.1. Its output retains original node labels; only the factorization ordering changes.



Algorithm 5.1: Forward I-MAP construction and effect extraction.


Input: Original DAG \(\mathcal D\), admissible \((L,D)\) with positive variances, treatment \(d\), outcome \(y\), and \(d\in\operatorname{an}_{\mathcal D}(y)\).
Output: Effect ordering \(\pi^*\), graph-defined I-MAP \(G^*\) and constrained parameters \((\widetilde L,\widetilde D)\).

Compute \(M=\operatorname{de}(d)\cap\operatorname{an}(y)\) and a closest topological ordering \(\pi_{dy}=\langle\delta_1,d,M,y,\delta_3\rangle\) as above.
Initialize \((\widetilde L,\widetilde D)\leftarrow(L,D)\) and the current ordering to \(\pi_{dy}\).
For each \(m\) in reverse order of the mediator block: transpose the adjacent pair \((m,y)\) using Section 5.3, saving the old variances; exchange their positions in the current ordering even if the coefficient is zero.
For each node \(j\) and predecessor \(u\) in the resulting ordering, add \(u\to j\) to \(G^*\) exactly when \(u\) and \(j\) are not d-separated in \(\mathcal D\) by the other predecessors.
Return \(\pi^*=\langle\delta_1,d,y,M,\delta_3\rangle\), \(G^*\) and \((\widetilde L,\widetilde D)\); read \(\tau_{dy}=-\widetilde L_{dy}\).




Start with a closest ordering. Traverse \(M\) in reverse topological order and transpose each mediator with \(y\). At every step they are adjacent. If the current coefficient happens to be zero, swap their ordering with no numerical change. After the last step, the ordering is \(\pi^*\) and the parameters are its unique Gaussian regression factorization. Minimality relative to the original graph follows from the ordered d-separation criterion; it does not follow solely from a succession of locally minimal I-MAPs.
To reverse the construction, traverse \(M\) in its original topological order, transposing \(y\) with each mediator. Each transposition is an involution on its adjacent factorization pair: alternatively, uniqueness in the restored ordering proves that the reverse sequence recovers the original \((L,D)\) on the constrained image. Applied to an unconstrained Gaussian factorization on \(G^*\), it recovers a factorization in \(\pi_{dy}\) that can have extra coefficients.



Algorithm 5.2: Reverse factorization and sparse-model membership.


Input: Original \(\mathcal D\) and closest ordering \(\pi_{dy}\); a positive-variance factorization \((\widetilde L,\widetilde D)\) on \(G^*\) in ordering \(\pi^*\).
Output: Restored \((L^{\mathrm{back}},D^{\mathrm{back}})\) and exact membership condition for the original model.

Initialize the current parameters to \((\widetilde L,\widetilde D)\) and ordering to \(\pi^*\).
For each \(m\) in the original topological mediator order: transpose the adjacent pair \((y,m)\) and exchange their positions.
Collect \(L^{\mathrm{back}}_{uv}\) for every original-order pair \(u\prec_{\pi_{dy}}v\) whose edge \(u\to v\) is absent from \(\mathcal D\).
Return the restored parameters and the condition that every collected coefficient equals zero. In numerical evaluation, report an explicit tolerance rather than treating thresholded support as a graphical assertion.




With exactly one mediator, a single adjacent transposition in a closest ordering produces the effect coefficient. The existence of an edge \(m\to y\) alone does not imply that \(m\) is the sole mediator.

title: 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints
section: 5.5 Exact characterization of the constrained image
text:
5.5 Exact characterization of the constrained image
Let \(\Theta_{\mathcal D}\) have one free coefficient per allowed edge and \(q\) positive variances. Let \(\Theta_{G^*}\) be the analogous ambient space. The change of ordering \(F\) maps the former into the latter while preserving \(\Sigma\).
For \(\widetilde\theta\in\Theta_{G^*}\), reconstruct its covariance and factorize it in the original ordering, obtaining \((L^{\mathrm{back}},D^{\mathrm{back}})\). Then
\[
F(\Theta_{\mathcal D})=
\left\{\widetilde\theta\in\Theta_{G^*}:
L^{\mathrm{back}}_{uv}=0\ \text{for every }u\prec_{\pi_{dy}}v\text{ with }u\to v\notin E\right\}.
\]






NoteProof





Necessity follows from reversing \(F\). For sufficiency, the imposed zeros place the restored factorization in \(\Theta_{\mathcal D}\). Refactorizing it in \(\pi^*\) returns the unique original \(\widetilde\theta\). All denominators are positive conditional variances. Consequently \(F\) and its inverse are smooth on the positive-variance domains, and the image has dimension \(q+|E|\), even though the ambient I-MAP has dimension \(q+|E(G^*)|\). \(\square\)



This characterization avoids any need to infer constraints from a single numerical sparsity pattern. Constraints may be redundant; their number need not equal their rank. A choice of which entries to solve for can fail at zero denominators, so a global free-coordinate chart and variation independence of the effect from the nuisance parameters require additional conditions.
The construction preserves the observational model. The alternative arrows generally do not retain the original intervention semantics. The distinguished effect coefficient is justified by the preceding theorem; other intervention effects must still be evaluated from the original causal model.

title: 5  The I-MAP construction and its constraints
text:
5.6 A chain in effect coordinates
For \(1\to2\to3\) with structural coefficients \(b=B_{12}\) and \(c=B_{23}\), the closest ordering is \((1,2,3)\) and the effect ordering is \((1,3,2)\). Here \(M=\{2\}\) and \(O=\varnothing\). Substitution gives
\[
X_3=bcX_1+c\epsilon_2+\epsilon_3.
\]
Thus the transformed outcome equation has coefficient \(\tau_{13}=bc\) and residual variance \(s=c^2v_2+v_3\). In the regression of \(X_2\) on \((X_1,X_3)\), put
\[
k=\frac{cv_2}{s},\qquad u=\frac{v_2v_3}{s}.
\]
Its coefficients are \(b-k\tau_{13}\) for \(X_1\) and \(k\) for \(X_3\), with residual variance \(u>0\). These are the adjacent-transposition formulas expressed as regression coefficients. The unconstrained I-MAP has three edges; the original chain has two. Reversing the transposition enforces the one missing-edge equation, so the transformed model still has five free parameters.
The comparison in Section 2.3.1 uses the same causal marginal and preserves the chain by a different explicit constraint. Both representations expose the effect, and both must retain the original model’s restrictions. The diamond in Section A.1 illustrates the analogous construction with multiple causal paths and two missing-edge constraints.

title: 6  The fully Bayesian workflow
text:
6.1 A common effect prior and the structural null
A fully Bayesian analysis uses one joint model for the graph, its admissible parameters and the observations. Let \(\mathfrak D_+=\{\mathcal D:d\in\operatorname{an}_{\mathcal D}(y)\}\) be the active graph class and let \(\mathfrak D_0\) contain structural-null graphs. For an active graph, the I-MAP map \(F_{\mathcal D}\) exposes \(\tau_{dy}=-\widetilde L_{dy}\). It leaves the Gaussian likelihood unchanged and restricts the transformed parameters to \(F_{\mathcal D}(\Theta_{\mathcal D})\).
The workflow consists of specifying graph and parameter priors, computing graph evidence, learning or sampling the graph, drawing its conditional parameter posterior, and averaging the resulting effects. The intended computational target is a graph score inexpensive enough for repeated evaluation, together with a sampler compatible with that same score and prior. The exact baseline in Chapter 4 and the normalized tilt below give tractable reference cases. General effect-centered priors need additional integration methods.
Let \(H=\mathbf1\{\mathcal D\in\mathfrak D_+\}\). An explicit specification is
\[
P(H=1)=\omega_H,\qquad p(\mathcal D)=
\begin{cases}
\omega_H p_+(\mathcal D),&\mathcal D\in\mathfrak D_+,\\
(1-\omega_H)p_0(\mathcal D),&\mathcal D\in\mathfrak D_0,
\end{cases}
\]
where each \(p_h\) is normalized on its graph class. This allows effect inclusion odds to be chosen separately from the number of graphs representing each class. Conditional on each active graph, the aim is the same effect marginal \(h(\tau)\), with a graph-specific nuisance distribution. The unconditional prior on the effect is then \((1-\omega_H)\delta_0+\omega_H h(\tau)\,d\tau\). This statement assumes continuous active-effect distributions; extra point masses require a corresponding explicit specification.
Attainable effects. In the unrestricted Gaussian DAG coefficient space, every active graph permits every real value of \(\tau_{dy}\).
This argument uses the allowed zero coefficients; additional sign, magnitude or faithfulness restrictions need their own support analysis.
An effect prior cannot be arbitrary outside the attainable effect support of a graph. Even with support \(\mathbb R\), the nuisance-coordinate domain may depend on \(\tau\). A normalized conditional specification
\[
\pi_{\mathcal D}(\tau,\eta)=h(\tau)\,
q_{\mathcal D}(\eta\mid\tau),\qquad
\int_{\mathcal N_{\mathcal D}(\tau)}q_{\mathcal D}(\eta\mid\tau)\,d\eta=1
\]
provides the requested effect marginal in a valid chart. A multi-chart construction needs consistent densities on overlapping domains.
Analytical construction by reweighting. Suppose a proper baseline prior has effect density \(g_{\mathcal D}(t)\), and the desired density \(h\) is absolutely continuous with respect to that effect distribution. Then, almost everywhere under the baseline,
\[
\pi_{1,\mathcal D}(\theta)=
\frac{h\{\tau_{dy}(\theta)\}}{g_{\mathcal D}\{\tau_{dy}(\theta)\}}
\pi_{0,\mathcal D}(\theta).
\]
The practical obstacle is computing \(g_{\mathcal D}\) and controlling the ratio in its tails.
The chain in Section 2.3.1 supplies a simpler illustration. Draw \(\tau\sim h\), draw \(b\) from a proper continuous density with \(P(b=0)=0\), and draw positive variances from proper priors. Set \(c=\tau/b\). This defines a proper chain prior with the specified effect marginal. In original coordinates its density contains the factor \(|b|h(bc)\), multiplied by the nuisance density. The excluded chart boundary has zero probability under this construction, but can matter for numerical stability and for other priors. Locating an effect coefficient alone does not establish this normalization.

To see this, choose one directed \(d\)-to-\(y\) path, assign its first coefficient the desired value \(t\), assign its other coefficients one, and set every other allowed coefficient to zero. The path sum is then \(t\), and any positive variances give a valid model.
