title: 6  The fully Bayesian workflow
section: 6.2 Priors on the constrained I-MAP space
text:
6.2 Priors on the constrained I-MAP space
Possible prior construction. Normal/inverse-gamma local priors can be assigned to selected free I-MAP entries, with the remaining entries determined by the model constraints, to influence \(\tau_{dy}=-\widetilde L_{dy}\). Such a specification, denoted “I-MAP-Wishart,” requires an admissible coordinate domain and a proper joint distribution; the label alone does not establish a conjugate family.
A prior on the full ambient I-MAP generally assigns probability zero to the lower-dimensional constrained image. Choosing a collection of “free” entries requires a valid chart, its domain, a rule for all branches of the constraints, and a reference measure. Independent priors in two different charts usually induce different priors on the same covariance model. The diamond chart dividing by \(b'\) already illustrates a domain problem (Section A.2).
For a smooth bijective chart transformation \(z=g(\theta)\), densities representing the same prior obey
\[
\pi_z(z)=\pi_\theta(g^{-1}(z))\left|\det Dg^{-1}(z)\right|.
\]
For the embedded I-MAP image, work in coordinates of its actual dimension, not an ambient rectangular Jacobian determinant. A prior on the original DAG can always be pushed forward through \(F\); this preserves its marginal likelihood but does not independently choose an arbitrary marginal prior on the effect. Properness, effect support and the domains of a global or multi-chart nuisance specification must be established for each prior construction.

title: 6  The fully Bayesian workflow
text:
6.3 Laplace approximation and MLE invariance
Analytical identity. If a finite interior MLE exists, the constrained I-MAP estimate is \(F(\widehat\theta)\) by invariance under the smooth bijection onto the constrained image. It is not the unconstrained MLE of the denser I-MAP model.
For a proper smooth prior in \(k=q+|E|\) coordinates and a regular interior likelihood maximum,
\[
m(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)\approx
e^{\ell(\widehat\theta)}\pi(\widehat\theta)(2\pi)^{k/2}
|H(\widehat\theta)|^{-1/2},
\]
where \(H=-\nabla^2\ell\) is the observed information in those same coordinates. This MLE-centered expression is the leading approximation when the prior is smooth and positive nearby; a posterior-mode formulation incorporates prior curvature explicitly. Under standard fixed-dimensional conditions,
\[
\log m=\ell(\widehat\theta)-\tfrac{k}{2}\log n+O(1).
\]
BIC discards prior- and graph-dependent constants, so it cannot retain all effects of an effect-centered prior. Changing coordinates for a fixed prior does not change the exact integral; the transformed density and curvature terms compensate in the leading Laplace expression. Using the number of ambient I-MAP entries over-penalizes the model. A non-local prior that vanishes at a null maximum needs a separate approximation; the displayed regular formula cannot simply be used there.
Exact nodewise integration after changing priors is available only if the full prior and likelihood still factor into independent blocks in valid coordinates. The fact that some equations are numerically unchanged does not by itself establish that condition. A split between exact integration and Laplace approximation requires a specified prior and a factorization proof.

title: 6  The fully Bayesian workflow
text:
6.4 Graph search
For any properly specified score \(m(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)\) and graph prior \(p(\mathcal D)\), the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability is
\[
\min\left\{1,\frac{m(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D')p(\mathcal D')q(\mathcal D\mid\mathcal D')}
{m(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)p(\mathcal D)q(\mathcal D'\mid\mathcal D)}\right\}.
\]
Proposals can add, delete, or reverse edges, rejecting cycles. The skeleton-size prior \(p(\mathcal D)\propto\omega^{|E|}(1-\omega)^{q(q-1)/2-|E|}\) is a possible mass function on the chosen DAG space; orientation and DAG restrictions are part of that choice. Rejecting all moves that destroy \(d\in\operatorname{an}(y)\) targets a posterior conditional on ancestry. It cannot then estimate the probability of a structural null effect. A deterministic approximate marginal likelihood also targets an approximate posterior, not the exact one.



Algorithm 6.1: Metropolis-Hastings graph search for a specified evidence function.


Input: Proper graph prior \(p\), graph evidence \(m(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)\) for that parameter prior, known proposal kernel \(q\), initial supported DAG, and number of iterations \(T\).
Output: A graph Markov chain with the specified posterior as invariant distribution, subject to an irreducible proposal on its support.

Set the current graph to \(\mathcal D\) and compute \(\ell_{\mathcal D}=\log m(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)+\log p(\mathcal D)\).
For \(t=1,\ldots,T\): propose \(\mathcal D'\) using \(q(\cdot\mid\mathcal D)\); if cyclic or unsupported, record the current graph and continue to the next iteration. Steps 3–4 apply to each valid proposal.
For a valid proposal compute \(\ell_{\mathcal D'}\) and \(\log R=\ell_{\mathcal D'}-\ell_{\mathcal D}+\log q(\mathcal D\mid\mathcal D')-\log q(\mathcal D'\mid\mathcal D)\).
Draw \(u\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). If \(\log u<\min(0,\log R)\), replace the graph and its score by the proposed values; otherwise retain the current values. Record the current graph at every iteration, including rejections.
Assess convergence and mixing before using retained iterations for model averaging. Retain structural-null graphs if effect-inclusion probabilities are required.




Algorithm 6.1 is an inference specification; the exact small-graph experiments use enumeration. Substituting deterministic approximate scores changes its target. Random scores require a separately justified pseudo-marginal algorithm, not an ordinary substitution in step 3.

title: 6  The fully Bayesian workflow
section: 6.5 Conditional parameter sampling and model averaging
text:
6.5 Conditional parameter sampling and model averaging
For a fixed graph, sampling can use original free coefficients and log variances, computing the I-MAP effect within each evaluation. This automatically respects the missing-edge constraints. A density defined in I-MAP chart coordinates must be converted to these original coordinates with its chart Jacobian; log-variance coordinates add the factor \(\prod_j v_j\). Alternatively, a valid I-MAP chart can be sampled directly. Hamiltonian or other Markov chain Monte Carlo methods require a specified target density, branch handling and convergence diagnostics. Sampling every ambient I-MAP coefficient freely changes the model.
If samples \(\theta^{(s)}\) come from a baseline posterior under \(\pi_0\), reweight by \(w_s\propto\pi_1(\theta^{(s)})/\pi_0(\theta^{(s)})\), provided both densities are in the same coordinates and reference measure. If they instead come from the baseline prior, include the likelihood as well. Jacobians are needed when comparing densities in different charts. Support coverage and finite weight moments matter; effective sample size and tail diagnostics assess the reliability of the weighted approximation.
For posterior draws \((\mathcal D^{(s)},\theta^{(s)})\), compute \(\tau^{(s)}=\tau_{dy}(\mathcal D^{(s)},\theta^{(s)})\), assigning zero to every structural-null draw. Averages and quantiles of these draws describe the model averaged effect posterior; its mean is
\[
E[\tau_{dy}\mid\mathbf X]=\sum_{\mathcal D}p(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf X)
E[\tau_{dy}\mid\mathcal D,\mathbf X].
\]
Within-graph Monte Carlo weights and between-graph posterior masses must both refer to the same prior used in the scores. With reweighting \(r_{\mathcal D}=\pi_{1,\mathcal D}/\pi_{0,\mathcal D}\),
\[
m_1=m_0 E_0[r_{\mathcal D}\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D],\qquad
E_1[f\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D]=
\frac{E_0[f r_{\mathcal D}\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D]}
{E_0[r_{\mathcal D}\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D]}.
\]
These identities give a consistent route to evidence and conditional effect sampling. An estimated score used as if deterministic generally gives an approximate graph posterior. Exact pseudo-marginal sampling instead requires a nonnegative unbiased evidence estimator and an augmented-state acceptance rule that retains the current estimate; fresh random estimates in an ordinary acceptance ratio do not establish that target (Andrieu and Roberts 2009).



Algorithm 6.2: Conditional posterior reweighting and coherent effect averaging.


Input: A fixed DAG, proper baseline prior \(\pi_0\), new prior \(\pi_1\ll\pi_0\) in the same coordinates, exact baseline evidence \(m_0\), and \(S\) baseline posterior draws.
Output: An importance approximation to the new conditional effect posterior and its evidence.

For \(s=1,\ldots,S\): compute \(r_s=\pi_1(\theta^{(s)})/\pi_0(\theta^{(s)})\) and the original causal effect \(\tau_s\); structural-null effects are zero.
Set \(w_s=r_s/\sum_j r_j\), using stabilized logarithms. If all weights vanish, report failure rather than a posterior approximation.
Estimate \(m_1\) by \(m_0 S^{-1}\sum_s r_s\) and the conditional posterior expectation of \(f(\tau)\) by \(\sum_s w_sf(\tau_s)\).
Report weight dispersion, effective sample size and Monte Carlo uncertainty; examine support coverage and tails.
For model averaging, combine conditional reports with graph probabilities computed under the same \(\pi_1\). Evidence estimates used in graph search need the target qualification in Algorithm 6.1.

title: 6  The fully Bayesian workflow
text:
6.6 A normalized non-local alternative
Analytical result. Let a proper baseline prior on a fixed DAG be \(\pi_0(\theta\mid\mathcal D)\), with \(0<C_{\mathcal D}=E_0[\tau_{dy}^2\mid\mathcal D]<\infty\). Define
\[
\pi_M(\theta\mid\mathcal D)=\frac{\tau_{dy}(\theta)^2}{C_{\mathcal D}}\pi_0(\theta\mid\mathcal D).
\]
The corresponding marginal likelihood satisfies
\[
m_M(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)=m_0(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)
\frac{E_0[\tau_{dy}^2\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D]}{C_{\mathcal D}}.
\]






NoteProof





The baseline posterior density is \(p_0(\theta\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D)=p(\mathbf X\mid\theta,\mathcal D)\pi_0(\theta\mid\mathcal D)/m_0(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)\). Consequently,
\[
m_M(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)
=\frac1{C_{\mathcal D}}\int p(\mathbf X\mid\theta,\mathcal D)\tau_{dy}(\theta)^2\pi_0(\theta\mid\mathcal D)\,d\theta
=\frac{m_0(\mathbf X\mid\mathcal D)}{C_{\mathcal D}}E_0[\tau_{dy}^2\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D].
\]



This identity requires no I-MAP coordinates. The normalizing constant can be replaced by \(v\) only when the baseline effect marginal has second moment \(v\), for example \(\tau\sim N(0,v)\) in an admissible coordinate factorization. A general DAG-Wishart-induced path-sum prior need not have this second moment or even a finite one. DAGs with no \(d\)-to-\(y\) path have \(C_{\mathcal D}=0\); they require a separate null component rather than this tilt.
The tilted effect density is \(t^2g_{\mathcal D}(t)/C_{\mathcal D}\). It is therefore generally graph dependent. This tractable tilt illustrates effect-informed scoring, but does not itself impose a common moment-prior marginal across all active DAGs. For a specified common \(h\), the preceding \(h/g_{\mathcal D}\) construction is the relevant normalized reweighting.
The posterior second moment is exactly \(E_0[\tau\mid\mathbf X]^2+\operatorname{Var}_0(\tau\mid\mathbf X)\). A normal posterior approximation may replace these by \(\widehat\tau^2+\widehat V_\tau\), but \(\widehat V_\tau\) is not generally \(1/n\). For a regular parameter vector it is the delta-method quantity
\[
\widehat V_\tau=\nabla\tau(\widehat\theta)^\top H(\widehat\theta)^{-1}\nabla\tau(\widehat\theta).
\]
For an unconstrained Gaussian regression on a valid \(Z\), the corresponding OLS variance coefficient is \(\sigma^2_{y\mid d,Z}/\{n\sigma^2_{d\mid Z}\}\). Approximation accuracy near path cancellation and in small samples depends on posterior shape, prior moments and the model-specific information matrix.

title: 6  The fully Bayesian workflow
text:
6.7 Computational organization
For each proposed DAG, obtain a topological ordering, identify its treatment-outcome mediator block and construct a closest ordering. Fit the original DAG’s node regressions, then apply the adjacent column transformations to their parameters. This gives the constrained I-MAP MLE without optimizing a denser model. Each dense column update costs \(O(q)\), so moving the outcome across \(|M|\) mediators costs \(O(q|M|)\) once an appropriate factorization is available. Constructing that initial factorization and the graph’s score has its own cost; this bound is not a benchmark for a complete graph search.
Effect-centered priors can couple several equations, so nodewise score caching needs a factorization argument. Cache graph structures, sufficient statistics and genuinely unaffected score blocks; update the changed prior normalization as well as the likelihood. The same prior density, effect map and evidence conventions should be called by graph scoring and posterior sampling. Modular functions make this consistency inspectable.
The appendix includes an executable three-graph benchmark (Section A.6): compatible DAG-Wishart scores are equal for the chain and its two equivalent orientations, while a properly normalized effect-moment tilt can change their posterior weights. For this example, its normalizing constants and evidence corrections are computed analytically. It validates those calculations, without asserting that a general I-MAP prior is conjugate or that an approximation is uniformly accurate.






Andrieu, Christophe, and Gareth O. Roberts. 2009. “The Pseudo-Marginal Approach for Efficient Monte Carlo Computations.” The Annals of Statistics 37 (2): 697–725. https://doi.org/10.1214/07-AOS574.

title: 7  The two-step approach
text:
7.1 Discovery, adjustment and a common prior
The two-step approach uses an effect-informed discovery model to learn about graph uncertainty, then estimates the effect through a separate Bayesian adjustment regression. The motivation is to retain direct control over the effect prior while allowing a decision about which covariates to adjust for. Its output is a specified modular procedure, rather than automatically the posterior of the joint model in Chapter 6.
In the first step, a proper I-MAP prior and its marginal likelihood produce graph weights \(w_{\mathcal D}(\mathbf X)\). The active-effect marginal is \(h(\tau)\) and structural-null graphs receive their separately specified prior mass. The graph weights define which adjustment sets are possible or credible, but the union of graph-specific valid sets need not be valid across all supported graphs.
For a chosen candidate \(Z\), the second step fits
\[
X_y=\tau X_d+\beta_Z^\top X_Z+e_Z,\qquad e_Z\sim N(0,\sigma_Z^2).
\]
When \(Z\) is valid in the causal graph, the treatment coefficient equals \(\tau_{dy}\). Assign the same active-effect prior \(h(\tau)\), along with a proper prior \(q_Z(\beta_Z,\sigma_Z^2\mid\tau)\). The nuisance prior is part of the second-step model; it may change with \(Z\). If null uncertainty is retained, specify a point mass at \(\tau=0\) and its mixing weight as well. A continuous prior alone does not reproduce the structural-null component of graph averaging.
Equality of the marginal effect priors is the intended connection between the steps. A conventional normal/inverse-gamma regression prior usually specifies a normal coefficient prior conditional on \(\sigma_Z^2\), giving a marginal Student distribution after integrating the variance. That marginal must be checked against \(h\); using the same conditional scale or hyperparameter in two different models is insufficient. Independent \(h(\tau)\) and nuisance priors are one possibility, but may sacrifice conjugacy.
Both steps can use the same data if their output is declared to be a modular estimator or decision rule. This does not mean multiplying the first-step effect posterior by a second likelihood for those same observations: such a multiplication counts the observations twice unless justified by a joint model. A cut or other modular posterior needs an explicit definition of which feedback is removed. Splitting the data gives a different procedure; if a first-subset posterior is used as a second-subset prior, it is no longer the original \(h\). Matching priors therefore supplies comparability, not automatic joint Bayesian coherence or post-selection calibration.

title: 7  The two-step approach
text:
7.2 Choosing the adjustment set
The second step needs an action and a loss before an optimal adjustment set is defined. A possible action reports the posterior mean from each candidate regression and uses the first-step graph-and-effect posterior as a reference distribution for loss evaluation. This is a decision rule applied to the data, not an additional likelihood update. The admissible candidate collection can encode adjustment validity, computational cost or substantive restrictions. The O-set supplies a frequentist precision benchmark, while a Bayesian choice depends on the actual loss.

title: 7  The two-step approach
text:
7.3 A well-defined action space
An adjustment regression can be selected by minimizing posterior expected loss. Let \(\tau=\tau_{dy}(\mathcal D,\theta)\) have a proper reference posterior \(p(\mathcal D,\theta\mid\mathbf X)\) with a finite second moment. For each candidate \(Z\), specify a regression prior and obtain a reported number \(a_Z(\mathbf X)\), such as its posterior mean. This action is computable from the data and \(Z\); it cannot depend on an unknown true DAG unless a further, observable rule averages those DAG-specific actions.
“Bayesian OLS” does not by itself specify a posterior. A regression likelihood, prior, and treatment of the residual variance are required. A regression coefficient for an invalid set is an associational estimand, even if it is assigned a Bayesian posterior. The reference posterior for the causal effect and the candidate regression posteriors serve different roles.

title: 7  The two-step approach
text:
7.4 Squared-loss decision rule
Take \(L(Z,\tau)=(a_Z-\tau)^2\). Put \(\mu=E[\tau\mid\mathbf X]\) and \(V=\operatorname{Var}(\tau\mid\mathbf X)\). The exact risk is
\[
R(Z\mid\mathbf X)=(a_Z-\mu)^2+V,
\qquad Z^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_Z(a_Z-\mu)^2.
\]






NoteProof





Conditional on \(\mathbf X\), \(a_Z\) is fixed and \(E[\tau-\mu\mid\mathbf X]=0\). Expanding the square gives
\[
E[(a_Z-\tau)^2\mid\mathbf X]
=(a_Z-\mu)^2-2(a_Z-\mu)E[\tau-\mu\mid\mathbf X]+E[(\tau-\mu)^2\mid\mathbf X]
=(a_Z-\mu)^2+V.
\]
Since \(V\) does not depend on \(Z\), the minimizers are those of \((a_Z-\mu)^2\).



Analytical result. The chosen action is closest to the Bayesian model averaged effect mean among the available actions. The posterior variance of the reference effect is constant across \(Z\). The regression posterior variance \(s_Z^2\) does not appear. Thus squared loss for the reported point action does not separately penalize the candidate estimator’s variance. The full Bayes risk is not equal to its first term; that term is only an equivalent minimization objective.



Algorithm 7.1: Two-step adjustment selection under squared point-action loss.


Input: Data, a specified first-step graph-and-effect posterior, candidate sets, a validity rule, proper second-step regression priors with common active-effect marginal \(h\), and squared loss for a reported number.
Output: A selected adjustment set and its point action, interpreted as a modular decision.

Compute graph weights and the reference posterior effect mean \(\mu\); retain the null component when included in the first-step model.
Enumerate candidate adjustment sets and apply the prespecified validity rule using graph weights. If no set is admissible, return that outcome.
For each admissible \(Z\): fit its Bayesian adjustment regression with its specified nuisance prior and any null mixing component, and compute the action \(a_Z(\mathbf X)\).
Select \(Z^*\in\arg\min_Z(a_Z-\mu)^2\), with a prespecified tie rule. Retain \(V\) when reporting the full reference posterior risk.
Report \(a_{Z^*}\), the selected set, its validity probability and the scope of its uncertainty report. Do not multiply the reference posterior by another likelihood for the same observations.




Algorithm 7.1 implements the stated loss, not a separate precision penalty. Other losses change step 4 and require their own derivation.
With \(\mu_{\mathcal D}=E[\tau\mid\mathcal D,\mathbf X]\) and \(V_{\mathcal D}=\operatorname{Var}(\tau\mid\mathcal D,\mathbf X)\), the law of total variance gives
\[
V=\sum_{\mathcal D}p(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf X)V_{\mathcal D}
+\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D\mid\mathbf X}(\mu_{\mathcal D}).
\]
If one formally writes a DAG-dependent action \(a_{\mathcal D,Z}\), its risk is
\[
\sum_{\mathcal D}p(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf X)
\{(a_{\mathcal D,Z}-\mu_{\mathcal D})^2+V_{\mathcal D}\}.
\]
The constant term here is the within-DAG variance; the total mixture variance additionally includes between-DAG variation. This expression describes an action that observes \(\mathcal D\); it is not an implementable decision under graph uncertainty without an additional rule. If \(a_{\mathcal D,Z}=a_Z\) for every DAG, minimizing the first term recovers the preceding closest-to-\(\mu\) rule, with the between-DAG constant retained in the full risk.

title: 7  The two-step approach
text:
7.5 Validity, precision, and alternative losses
Proposals. Distinct objectives need distinct specifications. Possible choices include:

Restrict to sets valid in every DAG with posterior support, if such sets exist; that intersection can be empty.
Require \(P(Z\text{ is valid in }\mathcal D\mid\mathbf X)\ge1-\varepsilon\), documenting the chosen tolerance and the posterior graph model.
Use the decision criterion \((a_Z-\mu)^2+\lambda s_Z^2\) with a specified \(\lambda\ge0\) to penalize regression posterior dispersion. This is a new criterion, not a consequence of the original squared-loss rule.
Evaluate predictive or repeated-sampling risk with an explicit data-generating model if the goal is estimator bias and sampling variance.

Enumeration of candidates is one computational approach, not a demonstrated necessary or uniquely available algorithm. The union of graph-specific valid sets contains sets invalid in other supported DAGs. A graphical characterization of a Bayesian criterion depends on its particular loss and posterior specification. The frequentist O-set result optimizes a different quantity (Chapter 3).

title: 7  The two-step approach
section: 7.6 Structural null effects and shrinkage estimators
text:
7.6 Structural null effects and shrinkage estimators
Consider the shrinkage rule \(\tau^{PB}=P(\tau\ne0\mid\mathbf X)\,\tau^B\). Let \(H\) indicate an active effect model, with \(\tau=0\) under \(H=0\). Then
\[
E[\tau\mid\mathbf X]=P(H=1\mid\mathbf X)E[\tau\mid H=1,\mathbf X].
\]
This is a coherent squared-loss estimator if \(\tau^B\) is the conditional active-model posterior mean. If \(\tau^B\) is already the unconditional model averaged mean, multiplying by \(P(H=1\mid\mathbf X)\) applies the inclusion factor twice. If \(\tau^B\) is selected from adjustment regressions, the product needs its own loss-based justification.
Under absolutely continuous priors on original DAG coefficients, a nonzero path-sum polynomial equals zero on a Lebesgue-null set. Therefore, within an ancestor DAG, exact cancellation has prior and posterior probability zero whenever the posterior remains absolutely continuous; DAGs without ancestry supply a point mass at zero. This almost-sure relation does not say every ancestor parameter value has a nonzero effect. If graph sampling is restricted to ancestry, that structural-null uncertainty has already been removed (Chapter 6).

title: 7  The two-step approach
text:
7.7 A four-graph adjustment example
Take treatment 4 and outcome 6. Consider graphs with common edges \(1\to2\), \(1\to4\), \(4\to5\), \(4\to6\) and \(5\to6\), with these additional specifications:



Graph
Additional edges
O-set for the effect of 4 on 6




\(\mathcal D_1\)
\(2\to5\), \(3\to6\)
\(\{2,3\}\)


\(\mathcal D_2\)
\(2\to5\), \(6\to3\)
\(\{2\}\)


\(\mathcal D_3\)
\(2\to5\)
\(\{2\}\)


\(\mathcal D_4\)
\(5\to2\)
\(\varnothing\)



The set \(\{1\}\) is valid in every graph, since it blocks any back-door path through the treatment’s only parent. The set \(\{2\}\) is valid in the first three graphs, but in \(\mathcal D_4\) it conditions on a descendant of mediator 5. Likewise, \(\{1,3\}\) is valid in the other graphs but conditions on an outcome descendant in \(\mathcal D_2\). The union of graph-specific valid sets therefore includes inadmissible choices for some supported graphs.
For graph weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_4\), the posterior validity probability of \(\{2\}\) is \(w_1+w_2+w_3\). A rule requiring validity probability at least \(1-\varepsilon\) admits this set only when \(w_4\le\varepsilon\). A rule requiring validity in every supported graph rejects it whenever \(w_4>0\). Neither rule alone specifies the estimation loss, so it must be combined with a stated action criterion. Population regression checks for these examples are given in Section A.5.

title: 7  The two-step approach
text:
7.8 Posterior reports and uncertainty
After a point-action choice \(Z^*(\mathbf X)\), the selected regression posterior is conditional on that regression model and its prior. It need not include uncertainty from learning the graph or selecting \(Z\). An effect posterior obtained by averaging coherent graph models already includes graph uncertainty; a mixture of separate adjustment-regression posteriors needs its own weights and interpretation.
If the action is a distribution rather than a number, squared loss for a point estimate is no longer the appropriate specification. A proper scoring rule or an explicit interval loss can compare posterior reports, with validity and measurement costs added when relevant. Claims of efficiency, coverage or shrinkage improvement must be assessed for that complete procedure. In particular, a variance penalty cannot be inferred from the point-action squared-loss identity.

title: 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions
text:
8.1 Interpretation
The construction provides a precise outcome regression coordinate for the total effect while retaining every observed variable. Its extra arrows enlarge the unconstrained Gaussian model; the restored missing-edge equations recover the original sparse model. The target coefficient identity holds even at path cancellations, while the graph-defined parent set does not change with individual coefficient values.
This distinction explains both the appeal and the difficulty of Bayesian inference. The effect is easily located, but independent priors on arbitrary subsets of ambient entries do not automatically define a coherent prior on the original model. Chart choices, domains, normalization and Jacobians can matter. A pushforward of a fixed prior preserves Bayesian evidence; specifying new independent chart priors changes the scientific model.
crumbs: 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions

title: 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions
text:
8.2 Scope and limitations
The results concern one treatment and one outcome, Gaussian observational factorizations, positive error variances, independent errors, and a causal original DAG. They do not identify a causal DAG from observational data, extend automatically to hidden confounding or joint interventions, or preserve all intervention interpretations of the alternative arrows.
The O-set’s efficiency guarantee is asymptotic and frequentist. The Bayesian adjustment decision depends on its specified reference posterior and loss. Neither implies the other. BIC may approximate evidence under regularity, but discards prior constants; it cannot establish improved effect-prior calibration. Near null effects, non-local priors require appropriate normalization and approximations.
crumbs: 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions

title: 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions
text:
8.3 Comparison with frugal parameterization
Both constructions expose causal quantities, but the I-MAP result here focuses on a single mean derivative within a full-variable Gaussian factorization. Frugal parameterization directly organizes a causal distribution and its nuisance pieces under explicit smoothness and compatibility assumptions (Evans and Didelez 2024). Sparse-DAG comparisons require explicit constraints on the common observational model.
The chain in Section 2.3.1 remains non-redundant, but its displayed frugal blocks lose variation independence. The proof in Section 2.3.2 gives the corresponding I-MAP constraint and the consequences for independent ambient priors. Both require admissible nuisance domains, normalization and Jacobians. This shared difficulty does not imply that every sparse DAG loses variation independence or that prescribing an effect prior is impossible: other charts and conditional priors can work. Neither improved marginal-likelihood accuracy nor a complete graph-learning workflow follows solely from exposing a causal coordinate. Those properties depend on the constrained model, prior and inference method. The forbidden-projection approach also remains relevant under graph uncertainty: one can compute a projection within each candidate DAG. Marginalizing variables changes the inferential construction, but does not make that approach impossible (Witte et al. 2020).

title: 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions
text:
8.5 Conclusions
A total causal effect can be represented as a coefficient in an ordered Gaussian I-MAP, with outcome adjustment by the O-set. Adjacent transpositions compute this factorization, and reverse-order missing-edge constraints preserve the original DAG model. The observational reparameterization does not in general preserve the causal interpretation of every alternative arrow.
Bayesian inference requires more than locating the effect coefficient. The prior must be proper on admissible coordinates of the constrained model, and its density must transform with the appropriate Jacobian. A normalized second-moment tilt yields an exact evidence identity, while adjustment decisions depend on the specified posterior and loss.

title: 8  Discussion, conclusions and open questions
text:
8.6 Open questions
Effect-centered priors (Q004). When are nuisance coordinates globally variation independent of the effect? How can multi-chart or conditional priors accommodate path cancellation and zero-coordinate boundaries while retaining tractable normalization? How does the attainable effect support change under additional coefficient restrictions?
Evidence approximation (Q004). Under what conditions do Laplace approximations and posterior second-moment approximations remain accurate near null effects? How do prior sensitivity and importance-weight tails affect graph comparison?
Joint computation (Q004). Which admissible prior families support graph scores that can be repeatedly evaluated at useful cost and conditional samplers targeting those same priors? Can effect-informed scoring retain enough factorization for efficient updates without changing the intended sparse model?
Adjustment decisions (Q005). Which posterior loss captures the desired balance between point-estimation error, regression uncertainty and adjustment validity under graph uncertainty? What graphical or computational characterization follows from that loss?
Two-step uncertainty (Q005). How should a modular procedure report uncertainty after graph learning and adjustment selection? What calibration and sensitivity properties follow when the steps share an effect prior but use different nuisance models?
Parameterization scope (Q006). How can the explicit sparse-model constraints in I-MAP and frugal coordinates be used efficiently across graph search, and how do they compare with forbidden projection? Which parts of the construction extend to joint interventions or hidden confounding?

A.1 The four-node diamond
Take \(1\to2\), \(1\to3\), \(2\to4\), \(3\to4\), with treatment \(d=1\) and outcome \(y=4\). Write
\[
L^\top=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0\\a&1&0&0\\b&0&1&0\\0&c&e&1
\end{pmatrix},\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4).
\]
Thus \(a=L_{12}\), \(b=L_{13}\), \(c=L_{24}\), \(e=L_{34}\) and
\[
\tau_{14}=ac+be,\qquad O=\varnothing.
\]
The sign follows from \(B=-L\) off the diagonal: each causal path has two edges. Starting from \((1,2,3,4)\), transpose \((3,4)\) and then \((2,4)\) to obtain ordering \((1,4,2,3)\). Put
\[
s_3=v_4+e^2v_3,\qquad s=s_3+c^2v_2,\qquad t=ac+be.
\]
Analytical result. The resulting factorization, displayed in original node labels, is
\[
\widetilde L^\top=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0\\
a-tcv_2/s&1&0&cv_2/s\\
b-be^2v_3/s_3&cev_3/s_3&1&ev_3/s_3\\
-t&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
\widetilde D=\operatorname{diag}\left(v_1,\frac{v_2s_3}{s},
\frac{v_3v_4}{s_3},s\right).
\]
The last row represents \(X_4=tX_1+\widetilde\epsilon_4\). Both directed paths contribute to the outcome coefficient through \(t=ac+be\). All denominators are positive.

text:
A.2 Reverse constraints with arbitrary variances
Start with an unconstrained factorization in \((1,4,2,3)\),
\[
\widetilde L^\top=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0\\a'&1&0&f\\b'&h&1&g\\c'&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\widetilde D=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4),\quad w_j>0.
\]
To restore \((1,2,3,4)\), transpose \((4,2)\) then \((4,3)\). Define
\[
s_2=w_2+f^2w_4,\qquad t_4=\frac{w_4w_2}{s_2},\qquad
A=\frac{c'w_2+fw_4a'}{s_2}.
\]
The two restored coefficients absent from the original diamond are
\[
L^{\mathrm{back}}_{23}=h-\frac{gfw_4}{s_2},\qquad
L^{\mathrm{back}}_{14}=\frac{w_3A+gt_4b'}{w_3+g^2t_4}.
\]
Therefore the exact constraints are
\[
h(w_2+f^2w_4)-gfw_4=0,\qquad
w_3(c'w_2+fw_4a')+gw_4w_2b'=0.
\]
These polynomial equations include all positive variance values and do not divide by an edge coefficient. When \(w_2=w_3=w_4=1\), they reduce to
\[
h=\frac{gf}{1+f^2},\qquad c'+a'f+gb'=0.
\]
Solving the latter as \(g=-(c'+a'f)/b'\) is valid only on the chart \(b'\ne0\). At \(b'=0\), keep \(c'+a'f=0\) and \(h=gf/(1+f^2)\); excluding that case would discard valid parameter values. Unit transformed variances are a restriction on the example, not a harmless simplification covering every original model. The general formulas above allow arbitrary positive transformed variances.

A.3 Validation methods

A.3.1 Analytical methods
Structural substitution expresses the outcome as a regression on treatment and external parents of the causal nodes. Path polynomials distinguish graphically implied zeros from coefficient cancellations. Adjacent equation operations preserve the covariance matrix, and uniqueness of Gaussian regressions identifies the factorization in each variable ordering. Restoring the original ordering gives an exact missing-edge characterization of the constrained model.
Graphical I-MAPs are defined through the original DAG’s d-separations. Numerical coefficient support agrees with the graph-defined support under faithfulness; individual unfaithful parameter values can have additional zeros. All covariance factorizations assume strictly positive error variances.


A.3.2 Numerical validation
The base-R validation script independently computes d-separation by ancestral moralization and Gaussian factorizations by direct regression. The finite validation domain, coefficient and variance ranges, random seed and numerical tolerance are specified in Appendix A. The same script produces the tables and graph illustration.
The graphical checks concern all DAGs in the specified finite ordered class. Numerical checks compare population covariance factorizations, effect coefficients and reverse constraints. They assess the implementation against analytical benchmarks; they do not establish general theorems or the statistical performance of Bayesian estimators.


A.3.3 Reproduction
Run the validation from the repository root:
Rscript scripts/R/002-imap-validation.R
Standalone execution writes regenerated tables and execution-environment information to results/. The calculations use base R. A full HTML build executes the same validation code:
quarto render
The seed, inputs, parameter ranges and tolerances define the computational experiment; runtime information supports reproduction across environments.

section: A.6 A Bayesian evidence and sampling benchmark
text:
A.6 A Bayesian evidence and sampling benchmark
The Bayesian benchmark uses the three Markov-equivalent orientations of the path skeleton on \((1,2,3)\). Only the chain \(1\to2\to3\) permits the target effect of 1 on 3. It generates \(n=120\) zero-mean observations from that chain, with \(B_{12}=0.7\), \(B_{23}=0.9\) and all error variances one. The baseline uses compatible DAG-Wishart shapes with \(a=8\), \(U=I_3\) and equal graph masses. Seed is 20261012.
For the chain, the baseline coefficient blocks for \(B_{12}\) and \(B_{23}\) are independent. Therefore its prior and posterior moments of \(\tau_{13}=B_{12}B_{23}\) factor into the corresponding coefficient moments. In a node block, if the coefficient has conditional mean \(\mu\) and conditional variance \(vK^{-1}_{uu}\), with \(v\sim\operatorname{IG}(r,b_0)\), then
\[
E[B^2]=\mu^2+\frac{b_0K^{-1}_{uu}}{r-1},\qquad
E[B^3]=\mu^3+\frac{3\mu b_0K^{-1}_{uu}}{r-1},
\]
provided the required absolute moments exist. The benchmark has \(r>2\), which also gives a finite fourth moment. Independence then yields \(E[\tau^k]=E[B_{12}^k]E[B_{23}^k]\) for \(k\le4\).
Apply the properly normalized \(\tau^2\) tilt only to the active chain; keep the two null priors unchanged. Its evidence correction is exactly \(E_0[\tau^2\mid\mathbf X]/E_0[\tau^2]\). Its conditional posterior mean is exactly \(E_0[\tau^3\mid\mathbf X]/E_0[\tau^2\mid\mathbf X]\). These give independent analytical references for the evidence and sampling calculations. This tilt is not an assertion that every DAG has a common Gaussian moment-prior marginal.

A.7 Replicated effect-hypothesis comparison
The introduction’s Figure 1.1 is generated by the main simulation script, calling reusable functions in effect-testing.R. It uses seed 20261013, 200 independent replicated datasets per scenario, and nested sizes \(n=25,50,100,250,500,1000\). The chain and collider have coefficients \(0.8\), unit error variances and known zero means. All 25 labeled three-node DAGs are included, of which nine have a path from 1 to 3. The uniform graph prior is identical in the two analyses, giving active mass \(9/25\). Parameter priors use \(a=8\), \(U=I_3\) and the normalized effect-squared tilt on active graphs; null priors are unchanged.
No estimated graph score or graph MCMC is involved. For a directed path \(p\), let \(T_p\) be its product of structural coefficients. The exact moment is
\[
E_0[\tau_{13}^2]=\sum_{p,r}E_0[T_pT_r].
\]
Node blocks are independent under the DAG-Wishart prior and posterior. Each product \(T_pT_r\) uses at most two coefficients from any node block. For two coefficients entering \(j\), with conditional mean vector \(\mu_j\) in the \(B\) convention,
\[
E[B_{uj}B_{vj}]=\mu_{uj}\mu_{vj}
+\frac{b_j}{r_j-1}(K_j^{-1})_{uv},\qquad r_j>1,
\]
where \(b_j\) is the inverse-gamma rate, not an edge coefficient. Multiplying the relevant node moments and summing over path pairs includes covariance and cross-path terms. Both prior and posterior second moments are finite with the selected hyperparameters, so Section 6.6 supplies exact evidence corrections.



Algorithm A.1: Exact small-graph effect-hypothesis enumeration.


Input: Data, treatment/outcome, a finite DAG collection, compatible baseline hyperparameters and fixed graph masses.
Output: Exact baseline and normalized-tilt effect-inclusion probabilities, up to floating-point arithmetic.

Enumerate DAGs and directed treatment-to-outcome paths; classify graphs as active or structural-null.
Compute each baseline evidence and each active graph’s prior moment \(C_{\mathcal D}=E_0[\tau^2\mid\mathcal D]\).
Update the DAG-Wishart blocks with the data. Compute each active graph’s posterior second moment using the path-pair expansion.
Multiply active evidences by \(E_0[\tau^2\mid\mathbf X,\mathcal D]/C_{\mathcal D}\); retain baseline evidences for null graphs.
Normalize graph masses times evidences separately for the two priors, sum over active graphs, and obtain null probabilities by complementation.

The independent moment check uses seed 20261014 and 30,000 direct baseline parameter draws for each of the nine active DAGs, under both prior and posterior. It computes the effect using the separate three-node identity \(\tau_{13}=B_{13}+B_{12}B_{23}\) and compares its sampled square with the path-pair expectation. All 18 discrepancies are within seven estimated Monte Carlo standard errors; the largest standardized discrepancy is 1.95. This checks the moment implementation without using simulated integration to generate the plotted evidence. The earlier three-graph benchmark separately verifies compatible-score equality.
The plotted bands are empirical 10th–90th percentiles across datasets. Monte Carlo errors in this table concern the estimated replicate means; neither quantity is a posterior credible interval. A posterior cutoff would define a testing rule, but the figure alone supplies no general type-I-error or power guarantee. Its behavior depends on the effect size, nuisance parameters, hyperparameters and graph prior. In particular, observationally equivalent chain and fork truths give identical distributions of these outputs, as explained in Section 1.2.
